Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 4, 2025
Review Body: I listened to this book on Audible and it is absolutely fantastic. Every parent and grandparent should read this book. It should be mandatory reading. Social media is not benign. It is taking over our children and rewiring their brains causing permanent damage. It is vital we wake up to the hazards of social media and get control of it because our children are unable to do so. Their brains are not fully mature until they are in their 20s. And is our responsibility to stop the damage that is being done. We have moved from play-based childhood to digital-based childhood and the consequences are catastrophic. I don’t see how anyone could give this book under a five-star rating.

Review Body: This book truly articulated the shift in culture that we are seeing in society today with the proliferation of phones and expansion of the digital world. This book is such and important read for everyone, especially parents of young kids who are being raised in this new environment. His suggestions for collaboration by all to get a handle of this situation are spot on and need to be shared widely. Thank you for writing this book!

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 10, 2024
Review Body: Overall this was really good (and really sad, honestly) information about the world we live in. I think it is really critical that people know this information and act upon it. As far as his writing, he compares humans to animals A LOT which was a little annoying and talked a lot about evolution (which is his own belief and that is fine, but when applying to the masses I think he could have left all of that out and still made just as compelling of an argument). The overall message is crucial to read. I think a follow up book if you haven't already read it is Digital Minimalism to really affect change in your own personal life with screens. Another thing that bugged me was that he talked a lot about independence in children and I would love to know more about that especially as a parent of a girl because I want that for my child, but there are still evil people in the world.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on November 11, 2024
Review Body: The problem with this author is that he takes a small piece of a social puzzle or his personal experience and then over-expands that out to cover something as broad as the entire nation or an entire generation, when it simply is not true. His data is sometimes not even solid or is misleading. This book will make you think the generation‘s entire problem is social media, and it’s absolutely not true. Do we need more free range parenting, yes, but he could’ve covered everything he needed to cover in two chapters. Don’t waste your money. Get Gen Z, Explained: The Art of Living in a Digital Age instead by four Stanford scholars and published by the University of Chicago press. Do trust me on this.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 3, 2024
Review Body: This is exactly what I had been trying all along with my kids "Free play over video games, no cell phones, utilize time either solving complex problems or just sit and read any book, kids horseplay and test out the limits when they play with each other) I am glad this book is advocating the same things. This book won't do well in the UK since folks there are generally uptight (free play offends them) and like to control kids' behavior/boredom by offering them digital media. But this is a must-read for American kids and their parents so they can realize the hidden dangers of digital media.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 1, 2024
Review Body: As a former preschool teacher turned middle-aged parent of a teen, "The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood" hit me right in the feels. This book brilliantly dissects the chaos our digital world has thrown at today’s kids, making me nod in agreement and occasionally want to hug my old flip phone. It’s a compelling, eye-opening read that’s packed with insights, making it a must-read for parents, teachers, and anyone who’s ever wondered if kids these days really are different (spoiler: they are, and here’s why). Funny, poignant, and thought-provoking, it’s like having a coffee chat with an old friend who’s also a child psychology whiz. Highly recommended!

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 26, 2024
Review Body:
The Anxious Generation is a compelling and insightful exploration into the intricate relationship between social media use and the rising tide of mental health issues among today’s youth. The book adeptly connects the dots between the pervasive presence of social media in children’s lives and the corresponding increase in anxiety, depression, and other mental health challenges.

Haidt delves deeply into how the constant connectivity and digital interactions shape the psychological development of young people. Through a well-researched narrative, the book examines how the pressures of social media, from the quest for validation to the comparison culture, contribute significantly to mental health problems. The detailed analysis of how these platforms alter social dynamics and self-perception offers a thorough understanding of their impact on mental well-being.

What stands out in The Anxious Generation is its ability to present complex issues in an accessible manner, supported by both empirical data and real-world anecdotes. The book doesn’t just highlight the problems; it also prompts readers to consider potential solutions and approaches to mitigating the negative effects of social media.

For anyone concerned about the intersection of technology and mental health, The Anxious Generation provides a valuable and thought-provoking read, shedding light on the pressing issue of how modern digital environments are reshaping childhood and mental health.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on May 20, 2024
Review Body:
Social scientist Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation articulates details of a new psychological/social malady swiftly metastasizing in our culture. Wickedly, it begins in childhood, with the consent and abetting of adults. Smartphones, and other digital devices, “bring so many interesting experiences to children and adolescents that they cause a serious problem. They reduce interest in all non-screen-based forms of experience (author’s italics)”. This is the fundamental understanding at the core of the author’s thesis. Throughout The Anxious Generation, Haidt attempts to ask and answer in detail the following questions of the toxic cultural change we are living through: What has happened? How do we know it has happened? Why has it happened? What can we do about it?

Haidt writes: “I’ll show what governments, tech companies, schools and parents can do to reverse the disastrous transition from play-based to phone-based childhood.” He gives us a banquet of food for thought, but the elephant in the room remains: are citizens hungry for what he serves?

The book asserts that childhood’s necessary learning experiences have been curtailed by a cultural confluence of toxic events: safetyism that has moved from exclusive emphasis on physical safety to include now fears regarding emotional safety (safe rooms in colleges). Documented diminished confidence in faith-based and civil institutions also contributes to more disassociated adult human interaction.

“On the internet, everyone is the same age, which is no particular age. This the main reason why a phone-based adolescence is badly mismatched with the needs of adolescents…It all got worse during the COVID years of ‘social distancing’ and online everything.” According to studies reported by Haidt, “45% of teens report that they use the internet ‘almost constantly’…[This] has enormous implications for cognition.”

In 2017, Israeli psychologist, Professor Sam Vaknin, characterized the hording or paucity of hits on social media “like” buttons as a conditioning process, comparing it to the electrodes implanted in a rat’s brain to deliver a pleasure-jolt of dopamine. This conditions the rat to choose the pleasure bar instead of the food bar, and the rat will begin to starve itself. Vaknin, citing eating disorders and suicide statistics among teenagers, especially girls, stated that giving up addiction to social media is a two-step process that requires first, deprograming, and second, withdrawal. What has evolved is, en-masse, a serious mental condition, in kind with brainwashing.

Haidt offers potential solutions to the early, deleterious pre-teen exposure to smartphone dysphoria: 1. No smartphones before high school. 2.No social media before 16. 3. Phone-free schools. 4. Far more unsupervised play and childhood independence. The Anxious Generation says these goals probably might be effective. But will enough parents collectively agree to them? There is no current answer to that question.

Haidt writes: “The Great Rewiring of Childhood pulled young people out of real-world communities, including their own families, and created a new kind of childhood lived in multiple, rapidly shifting networks. One inevitable result was anomie, or normlessness, because stable and binding moralities cannot form when everything is in flux…The phone-based life produces spiritual degradation, not just in adolescents, but in all of us…In 2010 there was little sign of a mental health crisis. Now it’s all around us.”

--Tom Casey

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on May 14, 2024
Review Body:
Jonathan Haidt's "The Anxious Generation" explores how smartphones affect kids, urging parents to closely monitor tech use to protect mental health. He suggests delaying phone use, controlling internet access, and encouraging unstructured play. Despite slow societal change, the book sparks vital discussions on kids' well-being. Haidt warns of online dangers and urges cautious navigation of digital life. Despite challenges, he passionately calls for action to safeguard future generations. I 100% agree with him!!!

I thoroughly enjoyed reading this book & and I highly recommend it. It's a timely and essential recommendation for parents.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on May 6, 2024
Review Body:
I find myself talking about the key ideas from this book EVERYWHERE. This is a must read for every parent AND for every Gen Z who is wondering why their generation is struggling so much. The collective action Haidt recommends is the only way to reverse the trend of digital rewiring of brains caused by the onset of smartphones & social media (2010-2015) that has had - and continues to have - a devastating impact on the young people who are missing out on so much important growth (and sleep!!!) because they are on their phones. The opportunity cost of lost play & face-to-face social time is way too high.

Key take-aways:

Return childhood to mostly play-based, not the current phone-based. A healthy childhood is a phone-free one.

Give kids age- appropriate independence and responsibilities. Stop over-parenting & surveilling.

Give kids age-appropriate freedom to socialize privately in person so they don’t need to do it online (& be exposed to so many dangers that are far worse than what’s at the local park).

Take phones out of schools completely.

Normalize kids doing things liking walking to school and riding bikes to do errands.

As a longtime children’s summer camp owner, I can’t emphasize enough how great the campers & staff report feeling being free from their phones.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on April 26, 2024
Review Body: Jonathan Haidt, lays out a profound argument into the dangers of social media on the first generation to go through their most important developmental years with complete access to the online world. Haidt masterfully dissects the myriad factors contributing to the rising tide of anxiety among young people, from social media pressures to economic instability. With scholarly rigor and empathetic insight, he offers a compelling analysis that challenges conventional wisdom and prompts crucial conversations about mental health in the digital age. This book is a must-read for anyone concerned with understanding and addressing the anxieties plaguing the current generation. It will take a monumental community and parental effort to stem the oncoming tide. Excellent book. I challenge parents to read it before making judgments about the content. I also strongly recommend, The Coddling of the American Mind. We all need to do more to protect our children and grandchildren from these rising dangers to their mental health.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on April 25, 2024
Review Body: Haidt's work provides solid evidence for the problems of the digital age that plague our younger folk and society as a whole. More importantly, he offers common sense solutions to the issues he raises.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on April 4, 2024
Review Body:
Parent and public high school teacher here. I asked to have this bought for me after Dr. Haidt's interviews online. It's amazing.
While tangential to the mental illness affects of social media and the loss of play-based childhood development discussed in the text, allow me to present an educator's motivation for reading through the book...
I've seen direct evidence of the zombie-fying affect of smart phones on our kids. The addiction is real and runs deep. Even when students are forced to hang their phones in phone jails during class, they show obvious signs of agitation (separation anxiety) when we ask them to read through a simple passage or work through a mental process. They've trained themselves to open the screen, and search through google and youtube shorts and tiktoks until someone gives them the answer, blindly copying the answer someone else gave them. If this process isn't available, students get frustrated and give up, looking around to their peers for SOMEONE to give them the answer. The loss of free thought in schools is staggering (and for an educator, frightening)
When schools attempt to distance students from their smartphones, parents always bite back that they need to be in constant communication with their 17-year-olds in case something horrible happens. Parents must read through part 2 "The Backstory" and learn about how their helicopter parenting style has stolen many of their kid's grit and social endurance.

Now, as a parent that foolishly gave my hand-me-down smartphones to my kids I'm forced to confront my mistake and try to remedy this. I don't believe that things are too late and we as parents are now powerless to make changes. Dr. Haidt does present real strategies to accept our mistakes and being to reverse the damage we have done. Our kids lives (may actually) depend on us (the adults) to do the hard work of digitally detoxing our kids.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 31, 2024
Review Body:
I absolutely love Jonathan Haidt and pre-ordered this book because I couldn't wait to read and devour like I did the Coddling.

The research is spot on, the message is critically important (though I would say, I don't know that this message is limited to teens. I think Cal Newport's Digital Minimalism book is in order for adults too. The 24 hr news cycle is making us anxious too!) I digress. I love what he has to say about raising children and I have implemented a lot of these ideas with my four children already (disclaimer: Safety Minimalism gets the cops called on you for just letting your children play outside - at least near the suburbs of NYC where I live - but the confidence is a worthy trade off).

The only problem is evolution can't support these claims or sustain them. Evolution is a western-centric limited worldview that can only be described as a process of chaos and chance that has no particular purpose or meaning guiding it. In one of the photos of my review I addressed this when Haidt refers to hunter-gatherers to explain how important play is. The issue is that if evolution is "guiding" us, we can just evolve and adjust again to respond to the deathly threat of the digital revolution. There is no objective, absolute standard that says we must go back to our primitive ways, in fact- for whatever reason "evolution" got rid of play-based childhood and going back could be considered retrograde. Unless people were made with some purpose and design, we have no reason to go on this mission to save childhood. It will be selected out just like all other traits (how do we assume in evolution which traits are the good and which are the bad btw?). Evolution is a worldview that brings about change through death. We can't put all the digital issues of the age back in the box unless we are bold enough to claim that there is an objective standard of truth and morality.

Chapter 8 offers a view that some level of spirituality can "save us." I agree in a sense, but it can't be empty and made up or promulgated as an opiate of the people. God is not to be taken so lightly as our bandaid cure. We can have all of the excellent ideas of this book, without using the made up excuse that we are just mechanical processes to suppress the truth that we were created and designed by God to be saved from our sins only through Jesus' payment for them in his death and the promise of His resurrection. Lots of the world believes this, which is why I say evolution is very western hegemonic and atheistic in its nature to give us a good excuse to getting out of accountability from God.

All that said, I still really love this book and think it is very urgent and should be extended to all adults. But if we really are an unguided, mechanistic bunch of atoms bumping into one another, it really doesn't matter at all that the kids are not alright. They'll adjust. They'll "evolve." God help us.
